title: throughput-benchmarking-harness-and-methodology-wip-11
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures the current working methodology for throughput benchmarking of the serving runtime. Goal is to produce repeatable, comparable throughput numbers across model variants, instance types, and config knobs (batching, kv-cache, quantization). This is a living doc for the eng-serving-runtime team; it focuses on load generator configs, warmup/steady-state definitions, measurement practices, and common pitfalls we see during profiling and bottleneck investigations.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Use the harness to drive stable, latency-SLA-aware throughput sweeps.
- Separate warmup from measurement (explicit warmup phase of >= 3 minutes or until metrics converge).
- Collect both tail latency distributions and token-level throughput (tokens/sec completed).
- Fix seeds and loadgen payloads for repeatability. Store payload sets in "bench_payloads/vX" with commit hashes.
- Profile hot paths when throughput deviates (GPU utilization, kernel stalls, networking, scheduler backpressure).

Definitions and success criteria:
- Throughput (primary): measured as completed tokens/sec across all workers during measurement window.
- Stable window: a contiguous 60s window where throughput variance < 5% and p95 latency change < 10% vs previous 60s.
- Warmup: initial period to populate KV cache, JIT/kernal priming, CUDA memory paths. Not used for reporting.
- Repeatable run: same payload set, same instance type, same model ver, and same harness commit should produce results within +/- 3% across 3 independent runs.

Bench harness architecture (short):
- Coordinator (single process): schedules scenarios, aggregates per-worker metrics, coordinates experiment metadata and artifacts.
- Workers (many): generate HTTP/gRPC requests according to configured distributions, apply rate-limiting to realize target concurrency or QPS profiles.
- Collector: pulls Prometheus metrics from serving instances, collects GPU traces (nsys/ CUPTI) when requested, and stores logs + payload IDs.

Load generator configuration guidelines:
- Input payloads: use representative prompt mixes (short chat, medium single-turn, long streaming prefixes). Each payload file is a newline-delimited JSONL with fields: id, prompt, expected_max_tokens, deterministic_seed.
- Traffic model: prefer closed-loop for latency-sensitive SLOs and open-loop for peak throughput discovery. Document which one is used in metadata.
- QPS vs concurrency: specify target by QPS for open-loop. For closed-loop (N clients), specify N and think-time distribution.
- Rate ramping: 0 -> target in 60s linear ramp, unless finding burst behavior; document exceptions.
- Warmup config: minimum 180s OR until stable window detected; we recommend 5 minutes for large models or GPU cold starts.

Suggested default configs (examples):
- Small test (functional): payloads/smoke.jsonl, open-loop QPS=5, duration=120s, warmup=30s.
- Standard throughput sweep: payloads/standard-mix-v3.jsonl, open-loop QPS sweep [50,100,200,400,800], duration per step=420s, warmup=180s, collectors=prometheus+gpu.
- Saturation run: payloads/high-token.jsonl, open-loop QPS ramp to saturation with fixed step increments and 600s measurement per step.

Measurement and metrics to capture (always):
- Aggregated: tokens/sec, requests/sec (successful only), error rate, p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (generation completion), median token generation time.
- Resource: GPU utilization (per-GPU), GPU memory allocator stats (OOMs, fragmentation events), CPU load, network RX/TX, NIC drops, disk I/O (if model uses swap/paging).
- Scheduling: queue lengths (input queue, batch queue), average batch size, batching latency percentiles.
- Internal runtime: KV cache hit/miss ratio, KV cache warm fraction, fused-kernel usage counts.

Repeatability and artifact capture:
- Store the following in artifact bundle: harness commit hash, payload set id, serving image tag, instance type, kernel driver versions, pod/container runtime args, Prometheus scrape config, and raw request logs (ids + timestamps + latencies).
- Always run at least 3 identical runs for a configuration and report mean +/- stdev for tokens/sec and p95 latency.
- Attach checksums for payload files and include the seed values used for any stochastic samplers.

Warmup details and rationale:
- Why warmup: model serving involves JIT or kernel warm paths, attention KV caches that significantly affect throughput on repeated prefixes, CUDA memory pools that allocate lazily, and network path caches (connection pooling). Excluding warmup avoids reporting inflated numbers that only persist with cached state.
- Warmup strategy: replay a subset (~25%) of payloads with a sustained QPS that approximates expected steady-state average. If KV cache is a target dimension, include both unique and repeating prefixes in warmup to reach representative cache occupancy.

Profiling & bottleneck triage steps (when throughput is off):
1) Verify harness artifacts and payload checksums to rule out input changes.
2) Check Prometheus dashboards for abrupt drops or contention signals (CPU steal, mempressure, NIC errors).
3) GPU checks: nvidia-smi sampling + nsight-system trace for kernel launch latency and occupancy. Look for long CUDA memcpy, many small kernels (kernel-launch overhead), or serialization due to mutexes.
4) Runtime internals: enable flame traces of the runtime (a lightweight tracer we ship) to see where time is spent (scheduler, batch packing, token loop).
5) Network: measure request serialization times, TLS handshake rates, and connection churn.
6) Re-run with single-worker, single-replica to isolate inter-node issues.

Common pitfalls and notes:
- Results can be non-deterministic across driver/kernel versions. Record driver/kernel versions and repeat tests after driver pin.
- Small payload mixes favor latency-optimized paths and can underrepresent batching efficiency. Always include a realistic mix.
- Background noise on shared nodes (multi-tenant infra) can spike variance; prefer dedicated instances for SLAs.
- Batch size vs latency tradeoffs: report average and distribution of actual batch sizes seen during run.

Reporting format (what to include in perf ticket or PR):
- One-line summary: e.g., "Throughput for model XY on p4dn8: 1.72M tokens/sec (std 2.7%) at p95 132ms; dominant limiter: small-kernel launch overhead"
- Artifact link to full run bundle (S3/GCS), graphs (tokens/sec over time, tail latency over time, batch-size histogram), and key config snippets (harness commit, payload id, warmup duration).
- Short reproduction steps (commands to run harness + serving image) and which artifacts to collect for deeper triage.

Example harness snippet (YAML) to include in metadata: 
---
harness_commit: 7a3f9d2
payload_id: standard-mix-v3
mode: open_loop
qps: 200
duration_s: 420
warmup_s: 180
collectors: [prometheus, gpu, runtime_traces]
comments: "sweep step 3 on p4dn8, batcher config B2"
---
(note: above is stored as string_metadata in the bundle, not executed as-is)

Next steps / open questions:
- Validate that our "stable window" rules generalize to streaming generation workloads with very long prefixes.
- Add an automated detector that flags when a run's artifact bundle is missing driver/kernel metadata.
- Expand payload corpus to include multi-turn chats with server-side tool-calls to exercise branching execution paths.

Appendix: Quick checklist before a run:
- [ ] Confirm harness commit hash and payload checksum
- [ ] Confirm serving image tag and driver/kernel versions recorded
- [ ] Reserve dedicated instances (preferred) or ensure low-noise window on shared infra
- [ ] Upload expected artifact S3 path to harness config
- [ ] Warmup configured (>=180s for GPU-backed runs)
